## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read
- **list_projects** — List the caller's projects, newest first. Cursor-paginated

  further pagination.
- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read
- **list_projects** — List the caller's projects, newest first. Cursor-paginated
  (limit 1-100, default 20). Returns `ProjectRef` entries plus a `next_cursor` for
  further pagination.
- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a
  HyperFrames player widget that renders the project inline. Both the thumbnail
  and the preview HTML are regenerated server-side at request time.
- **get_project_status** — Text-only status check for an in-flight or finished
  project. Returns session_status (`p… [truncated]

Training monitoring in professional Australian football: theoretical basis and
recommendations for coaches and scientists

a
Human Performance Research Centre, University of Technology Sydney (UTS), Sydney, Australia; bCarlton Football Club, Melbourne, Australia


    ABSTRACT                                                                                                                    ARTICLE HISTORY
    Australian football (AF) is a high-intensity ﬁeld-based sport with regular collisions and intense physical                  Accepted 29 June 2019
    demands such as jumping, tackling and jostling, resulting in neuromuscular fatigue and soreness, combined
                                                                                                                                KEYWORDS
    with external stressors (i.e., sponsorship, education, family). These can inﬂuence an athlete’s fatigue and                 Australian football;
    recovery status, requiring an individualised approach to monitoring to optimise training readiness. Optimal                 monitoring; player
    readiness would reﬂect a condition where an athlete has no impairment of physical performance, no mental                    preparation
    fatigue or excessive psychological distress. A theoretical framework exists for athlete monitoring that includes
    the quantiﬁcation of training load and understanding individual ability to tolerate the training demands
    imposed by coaches. However, while this approach is thought to ultimately determine the readiness of a player
    for training and competition, it has not been tested empirically. The purpose of this review is to describe the
    theoretical basis that underpins athlete monitoring systems, and to provide an overview of their contribution
    to decision-making processes in planning and delivery of training in professional AF players. This review can
    assist coaches and scientists to gain a better understanding of commonly used monitoring measures and how
    the information derived from these sources is applied in a professional AF environment.

 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance", "Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of the theoretical basis for athlete monitoring in professional Australian football, covering training load (external locomotor and mechanical load, and session-RPE internal load), wellness questionnaires, neuromuscular screening tests (adductor strength, eccentric hamstring strength, countermovement jump, mid-thigh pull) and submaximal heart rate measures. The authors report that most monitoring measures have weak or incomplete evidence of validity, reliability and sensitivity to training load, and that links to match performance and injury risk are small or unestablished in this population. No search method is described.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a narrative review without a described search strategy, so the selection of evidence cannot be reproduced. The authors state that the monitoring framework has not been tested empirically in professional Australian football, so the review cannot show that any monitoring system improves readiness, reduces injury or enhances performance.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could over-read the review as evidence that the monitoring measures it describes are validated or effective for individual readiness decisions, when the authors state that most are not yet established.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "Ryan S, Kempton T, Impellizzeri FM, Coutts AJ. Training monitoring in professional Australian football: theoretical basis and recommendations for coaches and scientists. Science and Medicine in Football. 2020;4(1):52-58.",
  "doi": "10.1080/24733938.2019.1641212",
  "abstract": "This narrative review describes the theoretical basis for athlete monitoring systems and their role in planning and delivering training for professional Australian football players. It summarises commonly used external and internal load measures, wellness questionnaires and neuromuscular or fitness tests.",
  "tldr": "Monitoring in professional Australian football rests on a fitness-fatigue framework, but most monitoring measures lack established validity, reliability and sensitivity to training load. Use them together with coach expertise rather than as stand-alone readiness tests.",
  "methods": "Narrative review of the theoretical basis of athlete monitoring and the evidence for commonly used measures in professional Australian football. No systematic search is described.",
  "findings": "The authors report that external load (locomotor and mechanical) and session-RPE internal load show associations with subsequent running performance, but not clearly with football performance measures in competition. Wellness questionnaires lack established validity. Adductor strength and countermovement jump are reduced after matches but their sensitivity to training load is unknown. Eccentric hamstring strength is associated with later hamstring injury risk but has limited utility for acute readiness. Submaximal heart rate measures give an index of aerobic fitness over short periods.",
  "limitations": "The review is narrative with no described search, and it draws mainly on small studies from a limited number of clubs and seasons. The authors state that the theoretical monitoring framework has not been tested empirically in this population.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use locomotor and mechanical external load and session-RPE load when judging an individual player's readiness to train. Treat wellness questionnaires and neuromuscular screens as prompts for further investigation, and interpret them alongside other data. Check the validity and reliability of the specific protocols your club uses.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: use external load, session-RPE and a small set of neuromuscular or heart rate measures together to adjust acute training load between matches. The review does not show that these measures improve performance or reduce injury, so treat them as decision support rather than proof.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: this review does not address return to sport or injury rehabilitation decisions. It can inform readiness monitoring only in general terms and should not be used to clear an injured player."
 }
}

24	     Background: The optimization of athlete training load is not a new concept; however in recent years, the concept of “load
25	     management” is one of the most widely studied and divisive topics in sports science and medicine. Purpose: Discuss the
26	     challenges faced by sports when utilizing training load monitoring and management, with a speciﬁc focus on the use of data to
27	     inform load management guidelines and policies/mandates, their consequences, and how we move this ﬁeld forward.
28	     Challenges: While guidelines can theoretically help protect athletes, overzealous and overcautious guidelines may restrict
29	     an athlete’s preparedness, negatively inﬂuence performance, and increase injury risk. Poor methods, wrong interpretation of
30	     study ﬁndings, and faulty logic do not allow for systematic scientiﬁc evaluations to inform guidelines. Practical Solutions:
31	     Guidelines and mandates should be developed through a systematic research process with stronger research designs and clear
32	     research questions. Collaborating with statistical and epidemiological experts is essential. Implementing open science principles
33	     and sharing all sports training load data increase transparency and allow for more rapid and valid advancements in knowledge.
34	     Practitioners should incorporate multiple data streams and consider individual athlete responses, rather than applying broad
35	     guidelines based on average data. Conclusion: Many current training load guidelines and mandates in sports come from good
36	     intentions; however, they are arbitrary without sound knowledge of the underlying scientiﬁc principles or methods. Common
37	     sense guidelines are helpful when there is sparse literature, but they should be careful to avoid arbitrarily choosing ﬁndings from
38	     weak research. Without precise scientiﬁc inquiries, implementing training load interventions or guidelines can have negative
39	     implications.

     Background: The optimization of athlete training load is not a new concept; however in recent years, the concept of “load
     management” is one of the most widely studied and divisive topics in sports science and medicine. Purpose: Discuss the
     challenges faced by sports when utilizing training load monitoring and management, with a speciﬁc focus on the use of data to
     inform load management guidelines and policies/mandates, their consequences, and how we move this ﬁeld forward.
     Challenges: While guidelines can theoretically help protect athletes, overzealous and overcautious guidelines may restrict
     an athlete’s preparedness, negatively inﬂuence performance, and increase injury risk. Poor methods, wrong interpretation of
     study ﬁndings, and faulty logic do not allow for systematic scientiﬁc evaluations to inform guidelines. Practical Solutions:
     Guidelines and mandates should be developed through a systematic research process with stronger research designs and clear
     research questions. Collaborating with statistical and epidemiological experts is essential. Implementing open science principles
     and sharing all sports training load data increase transparency and allow for more rapid and valid advancements in knowledge.
     Practitioners should incorporate multiple data streams and consider individual athlete responses, rather than applying broad
     guidelines based on average data. Conclusion: Many current training load guidelines and mandates in sports come from good
     intentions; however, they are arbitrary without sound knowledge of the underlying scientiﬁc principles or methods. Common
     sense guidelines are helpful when there is sparse literature, but they should be careful to avoid arbitrarily choosing ﬁndings from
     weak research. Without precise scientiﬁc inquiries, implementing training load interventions or guidelines can have negative
     implications.

136	                                                                                                                           Introduction
137	
138	                                                                                                                                    Exertional fatigue is a physical and perceptual reaction that results in an increased effort to
139	
140	                                                                                                                           exert a given force and a decline in the ability to exert this force.1,2 Although peripheral mechanisms
141	
142	                                                                                                                           contribute to fatigue development during exercise, reductions in neural drive (i.e., supraspinal fatigue)
143	
144	                                                                                                                           with subsequent decrease in spinal motoneuron excitability also play a pivotal role.1,2 In this context,
145	
146	                                                                                                                           increasing motor cortex excitability by means of non-invasive brain stimulation has been suggested to
147	
148	
149	
150	
151	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 08/07/18, Volume ${article.issue.volume}, Article Number ${article.issue.issue}
152	                                                                                                                           enhance physical and mental performance.3 Together with transcranial magnetic stimulation, a main
153	
154	                                                                                                                           non-invasive brain stimulation technique is transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS),3 which
155	
156	                                                                                                                           consists of delivering a weak continuous electrical current to a targeted brain area using surface
157	
158	                                                                                                                           electrodes attached to the scalp. When applied over the motor cortex, tDCS has proven to increase
159	
160	                                                                                                                           corticospinal excitability 4 and sensory and pain thresholds in healthy individuals.5 As both decreases
161	
162	                                                                                                                           in pain tolerance6 and corticospinal excitability1,2 are related to the appearance of fatigue during
163	
164	                                                                                                                           exercise, tDCS might potentially enhance performance.
165	
166	                                                                                                                                    Although tDCS is gaining popularity for its potential ergogenic effect on athletic performance,7
167	
168	                                                                                                                           there is yet not enough scientific evidence to support its effectiveness, especially in the real-world sport
169	
170	                                                                                                                           context. Most studies have analyzed the effects of this technique on single-joint isometric exercises
171	
172	                                                                                                                           (e.g., knee extension, elbow flexion),7 and only in recent years have its effects on whole body dynamic
173	
174	                                                                                                                           exercise (i.e., cycling) been tested.7 Some benefits of tDCS have been reported, such as improvements
175	
176	                                                                                                                           in performance itself (e.g., power output or time to exhaustion) or decreases in the perceived effort for
177	
178	                                                                                                                           a given external load.8–10 However, the effectiveness of tDCS for the enhancement of performance in
179	
180	                                                                                                                           maximal incremental or time to exhaustion tests remains unclear,8–12 and to our knowledge only one
181	
182	                                                                                                                           study has analyzed its effects during self-paced exercise.12 Moreover, most research has been conducted
183	
184	                                                                                                                           in active or untrained subjects8,10–12 and only one study to date has assessed trained athletes (cyclists).9
185	
186	                                                                                                                                    Therefore, there is little or no evidence on the effectiveness of tDCS for enhancing endurance
187	
188	                                                                                                                           performance in elite athletes or in self-paced exercises. The main goal of our study was to analyze if
189	
190	                                                                                                                           tDCS could improve swimming performance (primary endpoint) in elite athletes. We also studied tDCS

521	                                                                                                                           Discussion
522	
523	                                                                                                                                    tDCS has proven to increase corticospinal excitability4 as well as to decrease pain perception,5
524	
525	                                                                                                                           with both factors being related to the appearance of exercise-related fatigue.1,2 In this context, we
526	
527	                                                                                                                           hypothesized that tDCS could enhance performance during a self-paced exercise such as swimming.
528	
529	                                                                                                                           Yet, our ﬁndings refute our original hypothesis.
530	
531	                                                                                                                                    Contrary to ours and other reports,11,12 a beneficial effect of tDCS on whole-body exercise has
532	
533	                                                                                                                           been observed in some studies, such as an improved performance (e.g., power output or time to
534	
535	                                                                                                                           exhaustion) or a decreased perceived effort for a given external load.8–10 This disparity of results could
536	
537	                                                                                                                           be caused, at least partly, by the large individual variability in the effects of tDCS on corticospinal
538	
539	                                                                                                                           excitability, possibly as a result of individual anatomical differences.26 Moreover, it has been suggested
540	
541	                                                                                                                           that the controversy on the effectiveness of tDCS for the enhancement of performance may also be due
542	
543	                                                                                                                           to the different electrode montages (i.e., cephalic vs. extra-cephalic montage) adopted in the scientific
544	
545	                                                                                                                           literature.7 Thus, placing the cathode over the shoulder might be more effective than its placement over
546	
547	                                                                                                                           the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, as the latter may impair the effect of the anode over the motor cortex.27
548	
549	                                                                                                                           Notably, as confirmed by recent evidence,10 an extra-cephalic montage –and not a cephalic one such as
550	
551	                                                                                                                           that used here– seems effective for the improvement endurance performance.

555	
556	                                                                                                                                    It has been reported that exercising (i.e., leg extension) to fatigue during ∼ 10 minutes (a
557	
558	                                                                                                                           duration similar to that of the swimming test performed in the present study) results in a decreased
559	
560	                                                                                                                           output of spinal motoneurons,28 which could be potentially attenuated by tDCS. However, the
561	
562	                                                                                                                           contribution of central and peripheral mechanisms to fatigue during self-paced exercise is duration-
563	
564	                                                                                                                           dependent. Thomas et al.29 observed a greater and lower peripheral and central fatigue, respectively,
565	
566	                                                                                                                           with short-duration cycling exercise (~6 minutes) than with more prolonged bouts (>30 minutes). Thus,
567

572	                                                                                                                           we hypothesize that tDCS could provide greater benefits on those exercise tasks where central
573	
574	                                                                                                                           mechanisms play a major role on fatigue development, that is, on activities of longer duration.
575	
576	                                                                                                                                    Notwithstanding, in the present study tDCS resulted in a higher vigor (which corresponds to a

578	                                                                                                                           higher score in the BRUMS items lively, energetic, active and alert), being this effect maintained after
579	
580	                                                                                                                           exercise. Subjective measures like the BRUMS have proven superior sensitivity and consistency for
581	
582	                                                                                                                           monitoring athletes’ well-being than objective measures such as blood markers,30 and a relationship
583	
584	                                                                                                                           between mood state (particularly vigor self-perception) and athletic performance has been observed.31,32
585	
586	                                                                                                                           Brandt et al.32 stated that new ways to maintain high levels of vigor in athletes should be explored, as
587	
588	                                                                                                                           lower levels of this mood status indicator are associated with a decreased chance of sporting success.
589	
590	                                                                                                                           To our knowledge, ours is the first study to report an improved mood state in athletes after tDCS. These
591	
592	                                                                                                                           results could be of great interest for athletes, as tDCS might potentially serve to improve vigor sensation
593	
594	                                                                                                                           before a competition. Further research is needed, however, to confirm the relationship between mood
595	
596	                                                                                                                           and performance.
597	
598	                                                                                                                                    Previous research in non-athletic (clinical) populations supports the beneficial effect of tDCS
599	
600	                                                                                                                           for the improvement of mood state.33,34 Kheder et al.33 observed a mood improvement in patients with
601	
602	                                                                                                                           fibromyalgia related to increased serum beta-endorphins levels after anodal tDCS applied over the
603	
604	                                                                                                                           motor cortex (C3 in the 10–20 EEG system, like in our study; Figure 1b). tDCS not only alters the
605	
606	                                                                                                                           functional connectivity of the region under the anode (in our case, the motor cortex), but also that of
607	
608	                                                                                                                           other cortical and deep brain regions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal,35,36 especially with the
609	
610	                                                                                                                           conventional methodology using two large sponge pads such as the ones used here (25 cm2). Thus, the
611	
612	                                                                                                                           spread of the electrical current from the left motor cortex (C3 in the 10–20 EEG system, see Figure 1b)
613	                                                                                                                            “Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Enhances Mood But Not Performance in Elite Athletes” by Valenzuela PL et al.
614	                                                                                                                           International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
615	                                                                                                                           © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.
616	
617	                                                                                                                           to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (F3 in the 10–20 EEG system, see Figure 1b), which plays a
618	
619	                                                                                                                           key role in mood and emotional processing,37 could explain the observed improved mood after tDCS.
620	
621	                                                                                                                                    On the other hand, no changes were observed on CNS readiness or HRV. It has been suggested
622	
623	                                                                                                                           that tDCS might influence cardiac autonomic regulation due to the role of the insular cortex on
624	
625	                                                                                                                           autonomic nervous activity.38 However, controversy exists regarding the effects of tDCS on HRV, with
626	
627	                                                                                                                           studies finding a shift towards vagal modulation,39 sympathetic dominance,40 or other authors reporting
628	
629	
630	
631	
632	Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 08/07/18, Volume ${article.issue.volume}, Article Number ${article.issue.issue}
633	                                                                                                                           no changes.38 Moreover, as tDCS has proven to increase brain excitability4, we hypothesized that it
634	
635	                                                                                                                           could influence the DC-potential, a marker of brain function that has been related to task performance,
636	
637	                                                                                                                           alertness or attention.20 However, no changes were observed in CNS readiness (which is calculated from
638	
639	                                                                                                                           DC-potential), at least with the user-friendly device employed in this study.
640	
641	                                                                                                                           Practical applications
642	
643	                                                                                                                                    Anodal tDCS applied unilaterally over the primary motor cortex is safe and seems effective for
644	
645	                                                                                                                           the improvement of vigor self-perception in elite athletes, which might be explained by an increased
646	
647	                                                                                                                           excitability of the motor cortex but also by the involuntary stimulation of other adjacent brain areas
648	
649	                                                                                                                           such as the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. However, this strategy provided no benefits on swimming
650	
651	                                                                                                                           performance.
652	
653	                                                                                                                                    Our study has some limitations. We did not recruit many participants, which we believe is
654	
655	                                                                                                                           justifiable given the difficulty of conducting research with high-performance athletes such as those
656	
657	                                                                                                                           assessed here (i.e., elite triathletes competing at international level). It is also noteworthy that our sample
658	
659	                                                                                                                           size was big enough to obtain meaningful results. Another limitation was the lack of measurements of
660	
661	                                                                                                                           cortical excitability or brain activity, which could have provided a deeper insight on the actual
662	
663	                                                                                                                           physiological effects of the tDCS protocol we used. Indeed, it has been reported that slight changes in
664	
665	                                                                                                                           this tDCS protocol (i.e., stimulating with 2 mA instead of with 1 mA) can result in opposite effects on
666	
667	                                                                                                                           cortical excitability.14 In turn, major strengths and novelties of our approach was the fact that we
668	
669	                                                                                                                           assessed elite athletes and the type of exercise performed (swimming), which allowed as to analyze the
670	
671	                                                                                                                           applicability and effectiveness of tDCS in real-world sport context. Future studies should test if tDCS
672	
673	                                                                                                                           could be effective for the enhancement of endurance performance on longer duration exercises.

677	
678	                                                                                                                           Conclusions
679	
680	                                                                                                                                    Anodal tDCS applied over the primary motor cortex did not improve swimming performance
681	
682	                                                                                                                           in elite triathletes but resulted in a marked increase of vigor self-perception that was also maintained
683	
684	                                                                                                                           after exercise.

                                                                                                                           Abstract

                                                                                                                           Purpose: This study aimed to determine if transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) could

                                                                                                                           be effective for the enhancement of swimming performance or mood state in elite athletes.

                                                                                                                           Methods: Eight male elite triathletes (age, 20 ± 2 years; maximal oxygen uptake, 71 ± 4 ml∙kg-
                                                                                                                           1
                                                                                                                            ∙min-1) participated in this crossover, counterbalanced, sham-controlled, double-blind study.

                                                                                                                           Introduction

                                                                                                                                    Exertional fatigue is a physical and perceptual reaction that results in an increased effort to

                                                                                                                           exert a given force and a decline in the ability to exert this force.1,2 Although peripheral mechanisms

                                                                                                                           contribute to fatigue development during exercise, reductions in neural drive (i.e., supraspinal fatigue)

                                                                                                                           with subsequent decrease in spinal motoneuron excitability also play a pivotal role.1,2 In this context,

                                                                                                                           increasing motor cortex excitability by means of non-invasive brain stimulation has been suggested to




Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 08/07/18, Volume ${article.issue.volume}, Article Number ${article.issue.issue}
                                                                                                                           enhance physical and mental performance.3 Together with transcranial magnetic stimulation, a main

                                                                                                                           non-invasive brain stimulation technique is transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS),3 which

                                                                                                                           consists of delivering a weak continuous electrical current to a targeted brain area using surface

                                                                                                                           electrodes attached to the scalp. When applied over the motor cortex, tDCS has proven to increase

                                                                                                                           corticospinal excitability 4 and sensory and pain thresholds in healthy individuals.5 As both decreases

                                                                                                                           in pain tolerance6 and corticospinal excitability1,2 are related to the appearance of fatigue during

                                                                                                                           exercise, tDCS might potentially enhance performance.

                                                                                                                                    Although tDCS is gaining popularity for its potential ergogenic effect on athletic performance,7

                                                                                                                           there is yet not enough scientific evidence to support its effectiveness, especially in the real-world sport

                                                                                                                           context. Most studies have analyzed the effects of this technique on single-joint isometric exercises

                                                                                                                           (e.g., knee extension, elbow flexion),7 and only in recent years have its effects on whole body dynamic

                                                                                                                           exercise (i.e., cycling) been tested.7 Some benefits of tDCS have been reported, such as improvements

                                                                                                                           in performance itself (e.g., power output or time to exhaustion) or decreases in the perceived effort for

                                                                                                                           a given external load.8–10 However, the effectiveness of tDCS for the enhancement of performance in

                                                                                                                           maximal incremental or time to exhaustion tests remains unclear,8–12 and to our knowledge only one

                                                                                                                           study has analyzed its effects during self-paced exercise.12 Moreover, most research has been conducted

                                                                                                                           in active or untrained subjects8,10–12 and only one study to date has assessed trained athletes (cyclists).9

                                                                                                                                    Therefore, there is little or no evidence on the effectiveness of tDCS for enhancing endurance

                                                                                                                           performance in elite athletes or in self-paced exercises. The main goal of our study was to analyze if

                                                                                                                           tDCS could improve swimming performance (primary endpoint) in elite athletes. We also studied tDCS

                                                                                                                           Participants

                                                                                                                            ). All of them were healthy, highly trained (~26–27 hours∙week-1) and competed at international level.

                                                                                                                           Owing to the gender differences in the current received during tDCS, with women receiving less current

                                                                                                                           at targeted parietal cortex than men when stimulated at identical current levels,13 only men were

                                                                                                                           included in this study. The study was performed during the winter season, before the start of the

                                                                                                                           competition period. Participants refrained from taking ergogenic aids or stimulants (e.g., caffeine) as

                                                                                                                           well as from doing intense exercise during the 48 hours prior to each testing session. They were

                                                                                                                           instructed to maintain their normal dietary patterns during the study. Participants signed an informed

                                                                                                                           consent form after the procedures had been explained in detail. The study was approved by the Local

                                                                                                                           Ethics Committee (University of Alcalá, Madrid, Spain).

                                                                                                                           Design

                                                                                                                                    A crossover, counterbalanced, sham-controlled, double-blind design was used. A schematic

                                                                                                                           representation of the experimental protocol is shown in Figure 1a. Participants attended the testing

                                                                                                                           facilities on two different occasions separated by one week. During each visit they received either actual

                                                                                                                           or sham tDCS. Each participant was tested at approximately the same time of the day (always in the

                                                                                                                           morning).

                                                                                                                           Procedures

                                                                                                                                    The tDCS session consisted of 20 minutes of anodal tDCS (BrainSTIM, E.M.S, Italy) at a

                                                                                                                           constant current of 2 mA with a 30-second ramp at on- and offset using two 5 × 5 cm sponge electrodes

                                                                                                                           soaked in 0.9% sodium chloride. The anode was placed on the C3 location in the International 10:20

                                                                                                                           System and the cathode was placed on the contralateral supraorbital Fp2 location (Figure 1b). The

                                                                                                                           research staff had undertaken validated training in landmarking the tDCS stimulator pads before the

                                                                                                                                    After the tDCS session participants performed an 800-meter freestyle swimming test which was

                                                                                                                           preceded by a standardized warm-up (i.e., 400 meters of light swimming freestyle, followed by four

                                                                                                                           repetitions of 25 meters all out interspersed with one-minute rests, and 200 meters of light swimming).

                                                                                                                           The start of the swimming test was marked with an acoustic signal, with participants inside the water.

                                                                                                                           They were encouraged to complete the test as fast as possible, but no specific cues regarding pacing

                                                                                                                           were provided. Two experienced coaches recorded swimming times each 100 meters with a stopwatch

                                                                                                                           (3x100, Finis, USA) and the mean of both measurements was used for analyses (difference between

                                                                                                                           raters for all measurements=0.08 ± 0.57 seconds; intra-class correlation coefficient=0.99). Speed was

                                                                                                                           analyzed both as raw (meters∙second-1) and normalized data (%). Normalized speed (%) was calculated

                                                                                                                           by relativizing raw speed to the average speed of the test. It has been proposed that analyzing the

                                                                                                                           diﬀerence between current and overall mean velocity reﬂects the pacing pattern better than overall

                                                                                                                           performance.17 The fatigue index was calculated as the ratio between the raw speed of the first and

                                                                                                                           second halves of the test. The rating of perceived exertion (RPE) after the swimming performance test

                                                                                                                           was determined on a 1 to 10 scale (Borg CR-10 scale).

                                                                                                                           minutes after the swimming test, respectively. Lactate concentration was measured with a portable

                                                                                                                           scale (0 = not at all, 1 = a little, 2 = moderately, 3 = quite a bit, 4 = extremely). Data were normalized

                                                                                                                           for the analysis by subtracting the baseline score to those obtained after the tDCS session and the

                                                                                                                                    Heart rate variability (HRV) was calculated from heart rate measurements taken at baseline and

                                                                                                                           immediately after the tDCS session. During measurements, athletes were lying supine and relaxed for

                                                                                                                           10 minutes, and all R–R intervals during the last 5 minutes were analyzed. The natural logarithm of the

                                                                                                                           root-mean-square differences of successive heart beat intervals (LnRMSSD) was calculated with a

                                                                                                                           specific software (Kubios HRV software, Finland). The LnRMSSD has been described as the most

                                                                                                                           reliable and practically applicable measure for the monitoring of athletes.19

                                                                                                                                    CNS readiness was analyzed at baseline and after the tDCS session via determination of direct

                                                                                                                           current (DC) potential using a novel device (Omegawave Ltd, Espoo, Finland). The DC potential,

                                                                                                                           defined as brain bi-potentials within a frequency range (0–0.5Hz) lower than electroencephalogram

                                                                                                                           frequencies, has been reported as a marker of brain status, being related to functions such as task demand

                                                                                                                           and performance, alertness or attention.20 Two electrodes were connected to the sensor and placed on

                                                                                                                           the athlete’s forehead and on the base of the dominant hand’s thumb. As with HRV, the measurement

                                                                                                                           was performed with the athlete relaxed and lying supine. A proprietary algorithm then generated a CNS

                                                                                                                           readiness score that ranged between 1 and 7 arbitrary units (AU), with higher scores reflecting a better

                                                                                                                           performance.21

                                                                                                                           points) and BRUMS scores (three time points). Greenhouse–Geisser correction was applied when

                                                                                                                           Mauchly’s Test of Sphericity was violated, and post hoc analysis (Bonferroni test) was conducted when

                                                                                                                           differences was calculated as partial eta-squared (ηp2) for condition x time interactions or as

                                                                                                                           standardized mean differences (Hedges’ g) for specific time points, and the obtained ES values were

                                                                                                                           considered small (ηp2=0.01, g=0.20) moderate (ηp2=0.06, g=0.60) or large (ηp2=0.14, g=1.20).23,24

                                                                                                                           Analyses were performed using a statistical package (SPSS version 23.0, IBM, NY) with the

                                                                                                                           significance level set at 0.05. The chances of finding differences between conditions were assessed with

                                                                                                                           certainly not; 1–5%, very unlikely; 5–25%, unlikely; 25–75%, possible; 75–95%, likely; 95–99%, very

                                                                                                                           likely; and >99%, almost certain.23 If the chances of having better and poorer results were both >5%,

                                                                                                                           the difference was considered unclear.

                                                                                                                           Discussion

                                                                                                                                    tDCS has proven to increase corticospinal excitability4 as well as to decrease pain perception,5

                                                                                                                           with both factors being related to the appearance of exercise-related fatigue.1,2 In this context, we

                                                                                                                           hypothesized that tDCS could enhance performance during a self-paced exercise such as swimming.

                                                                                                                           Yet, our ﬁndings refute our original hypothesis.

                                                                                                                                    Contrary to ours and other reports,11,12 a beneficial effect of tDCS on whole-body exercise has

                                                                                                                           been observed in some studies, such as an improved performance (e.g., power output or time to

                                                                                                                           exhaustion) or a decreased perceived effort for a given external load.8–10 This disparity of results could

                                                                                                                           be caused, at least partly, by the large individual variability in the effects of tDCS on corticospinal

                                                                                                                           excitability, possibly as a result of individual anatomical differences.26 Moreover, it has been suggested

                                                                                                                           that the controversy on the effectiveness of tDCS for the enhancement of performance may also be due

                                                                                                                           to the different electrode montages (i.e., cephalic vs. extra-cephalic montage) adopted in the scientific

                                                                                                                           literature.7 Thus, placing the cathode over the shoulder might be more effective than its placement over

                                                                                                                           the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, as the latter may impair the effect of the anode over the motor cortex.27

                                                                                                                           Notably, as confirmed by recent evidence,10 an extra-cephalic montage –and not a cephalic one such as

                                                                                                                           that used here– seems effective for the improvement endurance performance.

                                                                                                                                    It has been reported that exercising (i.e., leg extension) to fatigue during ∼ 10 minutes (a

                                                                                                                           duration similar to that of the swimming test performed in the present study) results in a decreased

                                                                                                                           output of spinal motoneurons,28 which could be potentially attenuated by tDCS. However, the

                                                                                                                           contribution of central and peripheral mechanisms to fatigue during self-paced exercise is duration-

                                                                                                                           dependent. Thomas et al.29 observed a greater and lower peripheral and central fatigue, respectively,

                                                                                                                           with short-duration cycling exercise (~6 minutes) than with more prolonged bouts (>30 minutes). Thus,
