                                                                                                                           we hypothesize that tDCS could provide greater benefits on those exercise tasks where central

                                                                                                                           mechanisms play a major role on fatigue development, that is, on activities of longer duration.

                                                                                                                                    Notwithstanding, in the present study tDCS resulted in a higher vigor (which corresponds to a

                                                                                                                           higher score in the BRUMS items lively, energetic, active and alert), being this effect maintained after

                                                                                                                           exercise. Subjective measures like the BRUMS have proven superior sensitivity and consistency for

                                                                                                                           monitoring athletes’ well-being than objective measures such as blood markers,30 and a relationship

                                                                                                                           between mood state (particularly vigor self-perception) and athletic performance has been observed.31,32

                                                                                                                           Brandt et al.32 stated that new ways to maintain high levels of vigor in athletes should be explored, as

                                                                                                                           lower levels of this mood status indicator are associated with a decreased chance of sporting success.

                                                                                                                           To our knowledge, ours is the first study to report an improved mood state in athletes after tDCS. These

                                                                                                                           results could be of great interest for athletes, as tDCS might potentially serve to improve vigor sensation

                                                                                                                           before a competition. Further research is needed, however, to confirm the relationship between mood

                                                                                                                           and performance.

                                                                                                                                    Previous research in non-athletic (clinical) populations supports the beneficial effect of tDCS

                                                                                                                           for the improvement of mood state.33,34 Kheder et al.33 observed a mood improvement in patients with

                                                                                                                           fibromyalgia related to increased serum beta-endorphins levels after anodal tDCS applied over the

                                                                                                                           motor cortex (C3 in the 10–20 EEG system, like in our study; Figure 1b). tDCS not only alters the

                                                                                                                           functional connectivity of the region under the anode (in our case, the motor cortex), but also that of

                                                                                                                           other cortical and deep brain regions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal,35,36 especially with the

                                                                                                                           conventional methodology using two large sponge pads such as the ones used here (25 cm2). Thus, the

                                                                                                                           spread of the electrical current from the left motor cortex (C3 in the 10–20 EEG system, see Figure 1b)
                                                                                                                            “Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Enhances Mood But Not Performance in Elite Athletes” by Valenzuela PL et al.
                                                                                                                           International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
                                                                                                                           © 2018 Human Kinetics, Inc.

                                                                                                                           to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (F3 in the 10–20 EEG system, see Figure 1b), which plays a

                                                                                                                           key role in mood and emotional processing,37 could explain the observed improved mood after tDCS.

                                                                                                                                    On the other hand, no changes were observed on CNS readiness or HRV. It has been suggested

                                                                                                                           that tDCS might influence cardiac autonomic regulation due to the role of the insular cortex on

                                                                                                                           autonomic nervous activity.38 However, controversy exists regarding the effects of tDCS on HRV, with

                                                                                                                           studies finding a shift towards vagal modulation,39 sympathetic dominance,40 or other authors reporting




Downloaded by t_lambrinides@yahoo.com on 08/07/18, Volume ${article.issue.volume}, Article Number ${article.issue.issue}
                                                                                                                           no changes.38 Moreover, as tDCS has proven to increase brain excitability4, we hypothesized that it

                                                                                                                           could influence the DC-potential, a marker of brain function that has been related to task performance,

                                                                                                                           alertness or attention.20 However, no changes were observed in CNS readiness (which is calculated from

                                                                                                                           DC-potential), at least with the user-friendly device employed in this study.

                                                                                                                           Practical applications

                                                                                                                                    Anodal tDCS applied unilaterally over the primary motor cortex is safe and seems effective for

                                                                                                                           the improvement of vigor self-perception in elite athletes, which might be explained by an increased

                                                                                                                           excitability of the motor cortex but also by the involuntary stimulation of other adjacent brain areas

                                                                                                                           such as the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. However, this strategy provided no benefits on swimming

                                                                                                                           performance.

                                                                                                                                    Our study has some limitations. We did not recruit many participants, which we believe is

                                                                                                                           justifiable given the difficulty of conducting research with high-performance athletes such as those

                                                                                                                           assessed here (i.e., elite triathletes competing at international level). It is also noteworthy that our sample

                                                                                                                           size was big enough to obtain meaningful results. Another limitation was the lack of measurements of

                                                                                                                           cortical excitability or brain activity, which could have provided a deeper insight on the actual

                                                                                                                           physiological effects of the tDCS protocol we used. Indeed, it has been reported that slight changes in

                                                                                                                           this tDCS protocol (i.e., stimulating with 2 mA instead of with 1 mA) can result in opposite effects on

                                                                                                                           cortical excitability.14 In turn, major strengths and novelties of our approach was the fact that we

                                                                                                                           assessed elite athletes and the type of exercise performed (swimming), which allowed as to analyze the

                                                                                                                           applicability and effectiveness of tDCS in real-world sport context. Future studies should test if tDCS

                                                                                                                           could be effective for the enhancement of endurance performance on longer duration exercises.

                                                                                                                           Conclusions

                                                                                                                                    Anodal tDCS applied over the primary motor cortex did not improve swimming performance

                                                                                                                           in elite triathletes but resulted in a marked increase of vigor self-perception that was also maintained

                                                                                                                           after exercise.

                Review

                Transdermal Uptake of Substances Banned in Sports and Its
                Relevance for Doping Controls
                Sophia Krombholz1, Linus Korsmeier1, Mario Thevis2
                Affiliation addresses are listed at the end of the article.


                Abstract
                Transdermal drug delivery has emerged as an area of significant interest in both pharmaceutical sciences and antidoping research.
                This narrative review explores the implications of transdermal uptake of substances banned in sports, emphasizing its relevance
                for doping control analysis. The human skin’s complex role as both a barrier and a site of drug absorption is examined, alongside
                studies investigating the transdermal administration of substances on the World Anti-Doping Agency Prohibited List, including
                approved transdermal formulations and drug candidates. Recent cases demonstrate that (unintentional) dermal exposure of
                athletes to substances banned in professional sports, e.g., clostebol, can lead to an adverse analytical finding in doping controls.
                Consequently, studies investigating the detectability and metabolism of transdermally administered doping substances, which
                might even support identifying the route of exposure, are becoming increasingly important. This review emphasizes the relevance
                of addressing the skin as a pathway for both intentional doping and unintentional contamination, outlining critical implications
                for global antidoping efforts and future research priorities.

14	Treatment strategies for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries continue to evolve. Evidence supporting best-practice guidelines
15	for the management of ACL injury is to a large extent based on studies with low-level evidence. An international consensus group of

19	international experts on the management of ACL injuries, representing 18 countries, who were convened and participated in a
20	process based on the Delphi method of achieving consensus. Proposed consensus statements were drafted by the scientific
21	organizing committee and session chairs for the 3 working groups. Panel participants reviewed preliminary statements before the
22	meeting and provided initial agreement and comments on the statement via online survey. During the meeting, discussion and
23	debate occurred for each statement, after which a final vote was then held. Ultimately, 80% agreement was defined a priori as
24	consensus. A total of 11 of 13 statements on operative versus nonoperative treatment of ACL injury reached consensus during the
25	symposium. Overall, 9 statements achieved unanimous support, 2 reached strong consensus, 1 did not achieve consensus, and

Consensus Statement


Treatment After Anterior
Cruciate Ligament Injury
Panther Symposium ACL Treatment Consensus Group
Theresa Diermeier, MD, Benjamin B. Rothrauff, MD, PhD, Lars Engebretsen, MD, PhD,
Andrew D. Lynch, PhD, PT, Olufemi R. Ayeni, MD, PhD, Mark V. Paterno, PT, PhD,
John W. Xerogeanes, MD, Freddie H. Fu, MD, DSc, DPs (Hon), Jon Karlsson, MD, PhD,
Volker Musahl,* MD, and the Panther Symposium ACL
Treatment Consensus Group
Investigation performed at University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, USA

Treatment strategies for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries continue to evolve. Evidence supporting best-practice guidelines
for the management of ACL injury is to a large extent based on studies with low-level evidence. An international consensus group of
experts was convened to collaboratively advance toward consensus opinions regarding the best available evidence on operative
versus nonoperative treatment for ACL injury. The purpose of this study was to report the consensus statements on operative
versus nonoperative treatment of ACL injuries developed at the ACL Consensus Meeting Panther Symposium 2019. There were 66
international experts on the management of ACL injuries, representing 18 countries, who were convened and participated in a
process based on the Delphi method of achieving consensus. Proposed consensus statements were drafted by the scientific
organizing committee and session chairs for the 3 working groups. Panel participants reviewed preliminary statements before the
meeting and provided initial agreement and comments on the statement via online survey. During the meeting, discussion and
debate occurred for each statement, after which a final vote was then held. Ultimately, 80% agreement was defined a priori as
consensus. A total of 11 of 13 statements on operative versus nonoperative treatment of ACL injury reached consensus during the
symposium. Overall, 9 statements achieved unanimous support, 2 reached strong consensus, 1 did not achieve consensus, and
1 was removed because of redundancy in the information provided. In highly active patients engaged in jumping, cutting, and
pivoting sports, early anatomic ACL reconstruction is recommended because of the high risk of secondary meniscal and cartilage
injuries with delayed surgery, although a period of progressive rehabilitation to resolve impairments and improve neuromuscular
function is recommended. For patients who seek to return to straight-plane activities, nonoperative treatment with structured,
progressive rehabilitation is an acceptable treatment option. However, with persistent functional instability, or when episodes of
giving way occur, anatomic ACL reconstruction is indicated. The consensus statements derived from international leaders in the
field will assist clinicians in deciding between operative and nonoperative treatment with patients after an ACL injury.
Keywords: ACL injury; ACL reconstruction; nonoperative treatment

{
 "id": "Q05",
 "sourceFile": "Treatment after anterior cruciate ligament injury - Panther symposium ACL Treatment Consensus Group.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Treatment After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury, Panther Symposium ACL Treatment Consensus Group' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Consensus / Position Statement",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Consensus statement from the Panther Symposium 2019 ACL Consensus Meeting, in which 66 international experts from 18 countries used a modified Delphi process (an online pre-meeting survey, then in-person discussion and a vote) with 80% agreement set as consensus. The authors report 12 finalised statements on operative versus nonoperative treatment of ACL injury: 9 unanimous, 2 with strong but not unanimous agreement, and 1 (delayed surgery to allow temporary return to cutting and pivoting sports, 43.4% agreement) with no consensus. Anatomic reconstruction was favoured for active patients who want to return to jumping, cutting and pivoting sports, and nonoperative treatment with progressive rehabilitation was accepted for straight-plane activities.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is an expert consensus rather than primary evidence, and the authors state that most of the underlying literature is low-level. The statements are framed for active ACL-injured patients in general, so the recommendations cannot be applied to a specific athlete without the clinical assessment and shared decision-making they describe.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the consensus as settled evidence for surgery, when the authors describe most of the supporting literature as low-level and call for randomised trials with longer follow-up.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "Diermeier T, et al. Treatment after anterior cruciate ligament injury: Panther Symposium ACL Treatment Consensus Group. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;8(6):2325967120931097. Article number as printed; page range not printed.",
  "doi": "10.1177/2325967120931097",
  "abstract": "An international expert group used a modified Delphi process at the Panther Symposium 2019 to produce consensus statements on operative versus nonoperative treatment of ACL injury. Eleven of the 13 statements reached the 80% threshold in the abstract, and the recommendations address active patients by sport type, concomitant injury and instability.",
  "tldr": "Experts agree that operative or nonoperative treatment can both be acceptable after ACL injury. Active patients who want to return to cutting and pivoting sports should be offered early anatomic reconstruction after a period of rehabilitation, while straight-plane athletes can be managed without surgery if they have no persistent instability.",
  "methods": "A modified Delphi consensus. Sixty-six experts from 18 countries took part. Statements were drafted from a literature review, circulated in an online survey, discussed at an in-person meeting and voted on, with 80% agreement defined as consensus. Liaisons completed a MEDLINE review for each finalised statement.",
  "findings": "Twelve statements were finalised. Nine were unanimous, and two reached strong consensus, including shared decision-making (82.6%) and the influence of anatomic differences (95.7%). Operative treatment was preferred for active patients who want to return to jumping, cutting and pivoting sports (100%). Nonoperative treatment was accepted for straight-plane activities (100%), with surgery indicated if instability persists in daily life (100%). The panel did not agree that delayed surgery is an option for temporary return to cutting and pivoting sport (43.4%).",
  "limitations": "The authors state that most of the evidence is low-level, that few trials compare early surgery with rehabilitation and delayed surgery, and that data on concomitant meniscal or collateral ligament injury are limited. The abstract reports 11 of 13 statements reaching consensus, while the conclusion reports 11 of 12, and the results list 12 finalised statements.",
  "practicalImplications": "For active patients who want to return to cutting and pivoting sport, use shared decision-making, complete a structured rehabilitation phase, and refer for early anatomic reconstruction if instability persists or giving-way episodes occur. For straight-plane activities, a structured progressive rehabilitation programme is an acceptable first option. Do not plan a delayed reconstruction for cutting and pivoting sport on the basis of this consensus, because the panel did not agree on it.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: this consensus offers no performance-enhancement guidance. Its relevance is to the return-to-sport decision for injured athletes, including the risk of secondary meniscal and cartilage injury when pivoting sport is resumed without surgery.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: this consensus can inform return-to-sport decisions after ACL injury. It supports shared decision-making, staged rehabilitation before reassessment, and anatomic reconstruction for athletes with persistent instability or those who want to return to cutting and pivoting sport. It does not give return-to-play clearance criteria or specific test thresholds."
 }
}

1	                                                                                                                                                        Review
2	
3	
4	Treatment of Pectoralis Major Tendon Tears
5	A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Operative
6	and Nonoperative Treatment
7	Blake M. Bodendorfer,*† MD, Brian P. McCormick,‡ BS, David X. Wang,‡ BA,
8	Austin M. Looney,† MD, Christine M. Conroy,‡ BS, Caroline M. Fryar,§ MS, Joshua A. Kotler,k MD,
9	William J. Ferris,‡ MBA, William F. Postma,† MD, and Edward S. Chang,§ MD
10	Investigation performed at Georgetown University Medical Center, Washington, DC, USA
11	
12	Background: The incidence of pectoralis major tendon tears is increasing, and repair is generally considered; however, a paucity
13	of comparative data are available to demonstrate the superiority of operative treatment.
14	Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this study is to compare the outcomes of operative and nonoperative treatment of pectoralis
15	major tendon tears. We hypothesized that repair would result in superior outcomes compared with nonoperative treatment.
16	Methods: In accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, a
17	systematic review of the literature was completed by use of MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, Cochrane, EMBASE, and Web of
18	Science databases. We included English-language studies that had a minimum of 6 months of average follow-up and 5 cases per
19	study. The MINORS (Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies) was used to assess the quality of the existing literature.
20	Meta-analysis of pooled mechanisms of injury and outcomes was completed. Pooled effect sizes were calculated from random-
21	effects models. Continuous variables were assessed by use of mixed-model analysis, with the individual study designated as a
22	random effect and the desired treatment for comparison as a fixed effect. Bivariate frequency data were transformed via the
23	Freeman-Tukey log-linear transformation for variance stabilization and then assessed through use of a mixed model with a study
24	level random effect and subsequently back-transformed. Significance was set at P < .05.
25	Results: A total of 23 articles with 664 injuries met the inclusion criteria for comparison. All patients were male, with an average
26	age of 31.48 years; 63.2% of injuries occurred during weight training, and the average follow-up was 37.02 months. Included
27	studies had moderately high methodological quality. Operative treatment was significantly superior to nonoperative treatment,
28	with relative improvements of functional outcome by 23.33% (0.70 improvement by Bak criteria which is scored 1-4; P ¼ .027),
29	full isometric strength 77.07% (P < .001), isokinetic strength 28.86% (P < .001) compared with the uninjured arm, cosmesis
30	satisfaction 13.79% (P ¼ .037), and resting deformity 98.85% (P < .001). The overall complication rate for operative treatment
31	was 14.21%, including a 3.08% rate of rerupture.
32	Conclusion: Pectoralis major tendon repair resulted in significantly superior outcomes compared with nonoperative treatment,
33	with an associated 14.21% complication rate. Statistically significant improvements were noted in functional outcome, isokinetic
34	strength, isometric strength, cosmesis, and resting deformity.

Review


Treatment of Pectoralis Major Tendon Tears
A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Operative
and Nonoperative Treatment
Blake M. Bodendorfer,*† MD, Brian P. McCormick,‡ BS, David X. Wang,‡ BA,
Austin M. Looney,† MD, Christine M. Conroy,‡ BS, Caroline M. Fryar,§ MS, Joshua A. Kotler,k MD,
William J. Ferris,‡ MBA, William F. Postma,† MD, and Edward S. Chang,§ MD
Investigation performed at Georgetown University Medical Center, Washington, DC, USA

Background: The incidence of pectoralis major tendon tears is increasing, and repair is generally considered; however, a paucity
of comparative data are available to demonstrate the superiority of operative treatment.
Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this study is to compare the outcomes of operative and nonoperative treatment of pectoralis
major tendon tears. We hypothesized that repair would result in superior outcomes compared with nonoperative treatment.
Methods: In accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, a
systematic review of the literature was completed by use of MEDLINE, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, Cochrane, EMBASE, and Web of
Science databases. We included English-language studies that had a minimum of 6 months of average follow-up and 5 cases per
study. The MINORS (Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies) was used to assess the quality of the existing literature.
Meta-analysis of pooled mechanisms of injury and outcomes was completed. Pooled effect sizes were calculated from random-
effects models. Continuous variables were assessed by use of mixed-model analysis, with the individual study designated as a
random effect and the desired treatment for comparison as a fixed effect. Bivariate frequency data were transformed via the
Freeman-Tukey log-linear transformation for variance stabilization and then assessed through use of a mixed model with a study
level random effect and subsequently back-transformed. Significance was set at P < .05.
Results: A total of 23 articles with 664 injuries met the inclusion criteria for comparison. All patients were male, with an average
age of 31.48 years; 63.2% of injuries occurred during weight training, and the average follow-up was 37.02 months. Included
studies had moderately high methodological quality. Operative treatment was significantly superior to nonoperative treatment,
with relative improvements of functional outcome by 23.33% (0.70 improvement by Bak criteria which is scored 1-4; P ¼ .027),
full isometric strength 77.07% (P < .001), isokinetic strength 28.86% (P < .001) compared with the uninjured arm, cosmesis
satisfaction 13.79% (P ¼ .037), and resting deformity 98.85% (P < .001). The overall complication rate for operative treatment
was 14.21%, including a 3.08% rate of rerupture.
Conclusion: Pectoralis major tendon repair resulted in significantly superior outcomes compared with nonoperative treatment,
with an associated 14.21% complication rate. Statistically significant improvements were noted in functional outcome, isokinetic
strength, isometric strength, cosmesis, and resting deformity.
Keywords: pectoralis major tendon tear; repair; operative treatment; nonoperative treatment

 "studyDesign": "Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": ["Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Rugby"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Male Athletes", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Prospective injury surveillance of the English Premiership (men's professional rugby union) over 16 seasons from 2002/03 to 2018/19. The sample was a mean of 576 consenting players per season from 16 clubs, with 124,953 match hours and 10,851 time-loss match injuries. The authors report a stable match injury incidence of 87 per 1000 hours, rising mean and median severity (mean 25 days) and burden, and rising concussion incidence, severity and burden. Concussion was the most common injury from 2011 onwards, and the tackle caused 43% of injuries.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a descriptive surveillance cohort with no comparison group, and the authors state that the causes of rising severity cannot be determined from injury surveillance alone. Recording changed over the period (paper to web-based system, OSICS-8 to OSICS-10 codes, match report card checks from 2016/17), so some of the trend may reflect reporting or recognition rather than true change.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the rising severity and concussion trends as proof that the game has become more dangerous or that return-to-play rules are the cause, when the authors say surveillance cannot establish why they changed.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "West SW, et al. Trends in match injury risk in professional male rugby union: a 16-season review of 10 851 match injuries in the English Premiership (2002-2019): the Professional Rugby Injury Surveillance Project. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020. Online first; volume, issue and pages not printed.",
  "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2020-102529",
  "abstract": "Match injuries in English Premiership rugby were recorded across 16 seasons from 2002/2003 to 2018/2019 in the Professional Rugby Injury Surveillance Project. The study describes incidence, severity, burden and concussion trends over that period.",
  "tldr": "Across 16 seasons of English Premiership rugby, injury incidence stayed flat, but injuries got more severe and concussion rose sharply. Concussion and tackle-related injuries deserve priority in prevention and in return-to-play planning.",
  "methods": "Prospective surveillance of men's Premiership, National Cup and European Cup matches. Clubs recorded time-loss injuries (more than 24 hours) and exposure, and injuries were checked against match officials' report cards from 2016/17. Incidence, severity and burden were calculated per season and trends tested with linear regression and false discovery rate correction.",
  "findings": "Incidence was stable at 87 per 1000 hours (95% CI 82 to 92), with a mean severity of 25 days and a burden of 2,178 days per 1000 hours. Mean severity (beta 1.2 days per year) and burden rose over time. Concussion incidence (beta 1.2 per 1000 hours per year), severity and burden rose, and concussion was the most common injury from 2011. The tackle caused 43% of injuries, and the knee had the highest burden (493 days per 1000 hours). Running-related injury incidence fell.",
  "limitations": "The authors note that small systematic changes in the method occurred over the period and that the system moved from paper to web recording in 2012. Causes of rising severity could not be determined from surveillance data. The abstract dates the concussion rise from 2009/2010, while the Results give 2011/2012 for incidence and burden, so the start date should be read from the Results.",
  "practicalImplications": "Expect a match injury to keep more players out for longer, with a mean of about 25 days lost. Plan the tackle, knee, ankle and shoulder injury risk alongside concussion prevention, and use the published burden figures as benchmarks for return-to-play planning within the club.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: this surveillance shows the tackle is the highest-burden match event and that knee injuries cost the most playing time, which informs where to focus preparation and load management for professional players. It does not test any intervention, so it cannot show that a specific training change would reduce injury.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: the authors describe expected injury severities by body region and injury type that can guide club return-to-play planning. The study gives population averages only, and it does not set return criteria or confirm that longer stand-downs reduce re-injury."
 }
}

  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: the report describes repair and rehabilitation with return to golf at 5 months and to judo training without competition at 10 months. These are two individual cases with no return-to-play criteria, so the report cannot be used to set a return timeline for a triceps repair."

8	Options, Rehabilitation Protocols, and Return‑to‑Play Outcomes

15	Abstract
16	Purpose of Review First metatarsophalangeal joint sprains or turf toe (TT) injuries occur secondary to forceful hyperexten-
17	sion of the great toe. TT injuries are common among athletes, especially those participating in football, soccer, basketball,
18	dancing, and wrestling. This review summarizes the current treatment modalities, rehabilitation protocols, and return-to-play
19	criteria, as well as performance outcomes of patients who have sustained TT injuries.
20	Recent Findings Less than 2% of TT injuries require surgery, but those that do are typically grade III injuries with damage
21	to the MTP joint, evidence of bony injury, or severe instability. Rehabilitation protocols following non-operative manage-
22	ment consist of 3 phases lasting up to 10 weeks, whereas protocols following operative management consist of 4 phases
23	lasting up 20 weeks. Athletes with low-grade injuries typically achieve their prior level of performance. However, among
24	athletes with higher grade injuries, treated both non-operatively and operatively, about 70% are expected to maintain their
25	level of performance.
26	Summary The treatment protocol, return-to-play criteria, and overall performance outcomes for TT injuries depend on the
27	severity and classification of the initial sprain. For grade I injuries, players may return to play once they experience minimal
28	to no pain with normal weightbearing, traditionally after 3–5 days. For grade II injuries, or partial tears, players typically lose
29	2–4 weeks of play and may need additional support with taping when returning to play. For grade III injuries, or complete
30	disruption of the plantar plate, athletes lose 4–6 weeks or more depending upon treatment strategy.

Turf Toe Injuries in the Athlete: an Updated Review of Treatment
Options, Rehabilitation Protocols, and Return‑to‑Play Outcomes
Arjun Gupta1,2        · Priya K. Singh1,3 · Amy L. Xu1,4 · Rachel S. Bronheim1 · Claire M. McDaniel1 · Amiethab A. Aiyer1

Accepted: 18 September 2023
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2023


Abstract
Purpose of Review First metatarsophalangeal joint sprains or turf toe (TT) injuries occur secondary to forceful hyperexten-
sion of the great toe. TT injuries are common among athletes, especially those participating in football, soccer, basketball,
dancing, and wrestling. This review summarizes the current treatment modalities, rehabilitation protocols, and return-to-play
criteria, as well as performance outcomes of patients who have sustained TT injuries.
Recent Findings Less than 2% of TT injuries require surgery, but those that do are typically grade III injuries with damage
to the MTP joint, evidence of bony injury, or severe instability. Rehabilitation protocols following non-operative manage-
ment consist of 3 phases lasting up to 10 weeks, whereas protocols following operative management consist of 4 phases
lasting up 20 weeks. Athletes with low-grade injuries typically achieve their prior level of performance. However, among
athletes with higher grade injuries, treated both non-operatively and operatively, about 70% are expected to maintain their
level of performance.
Summary The treatment protocol, return-to-play criteria, and overall performance outcomes for TT injuries depend on the
severity and classification of the initial sprain. For grade I injuries, players may return to play once they experience minimal
to no pain with normal weightbearing, traditionally after 3–5 days. For grade II injuries, or partial tears, players typically lose
2–4 weeks of play and may need additional support with taping when returning to play. For grade III injuries, or complete
disruption of the plantar plate, athletes lose 4–6 weeks or more depending upon treatment strategy.

Keywords Turf toe · First metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint · Hallux rigidus · Return to play · Rehabilitation · Postoperative

 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Rehabilitation"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of first metatarsophalangeal (turf toe) sprains in athletes, covering the Anderson grading system, risk factors, imaging, non-operative and operative treatment, phased rehabilitation protocols and return-to-play outcomes. The authors report that under 2% of turf toe injuries need surgery, that grade I injuries usually return in 3 to 5 days, grade II injuries lose about 2 to 4 weeks, and grade III injuries lose 4 to 6 weeks or more. They also report that about 70% of athletes with higher-grade injuries, treated either way, are expected to keep their prior performance level. No search method is described.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a narrative review with no described search, and the return-to-play figures draw on case series, single-league surveillance data and small cohorts. The grading table and timelines are composites of sources, and the review notes that time to return varies widely with sport, position and level, so the numbers are typical values rather than criteria.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could take the 2 to 4 week and 4 to 6 week loss estimates as fixed return timelines for each grade, when the review shows return times ranging from days to many months depending on position, level and treatment.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Gupta A, Singh PK, Xu AL, Bronheim RS, McDaniel CM, Aiyer AA. Turf toe injuries in the athlete: an updated review of treatment options, rehabilitation protocols, and return-to-play outcomes. Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine. 2023. Online publication; volume and pages not printed.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s12178-023-09870-y",
  "abstract": "This review summarises treatment modalities, rehabilitation protocols, return-to-play criteria and performance outcomes after turf toe (first metatarsophalangeal joint sprain) injuries in athletes.",
  "tldr": "Most turf toe injuries are grade I or II and recover without surgery, while grade III injuries may need surgical repair and months of rehabilitation. Use the Anderson grade and the stated phased protocols to plan return, not a single fixed timeline.",
  "methods": "Narrative review of the literature on classification, risk factors, imaging, non-operative and operative management, phased rehabilitation (Tables 4 and 5), return-to-play criteria and performance outcomes. No systematic search is described.",
  "findings": "Under 2% of injuries require surgery, usually grade III injuries with MTP joint damage, bony injury or severe instability. Non-operative rehabilitation has three phases over up to 10 weeks, and operative rehabilitation four phases over up to 20 weeks. Grade I injuries usually return after 3 to 5 days, grade II injuries lose about 2 to 4 weeks, and grade III injuries lose 4 to 6 weeks or more. Median return after non-operative care was 5.85 weeks in one systematic review of 65 patients, against 14.7 weeks after surgery. About 70% of athletes with higher-grade injuries, treated either way, are expected to maintain their level of performance, and one NFL study found power ratings comparable to uninjured controls for low-grade injuries.",
  "limitations": "The review is narrative, so its selection of sources is not reproducible. Many cited return-to-play figures come from small case series, retrospective league data and one systematic review with a wide time range (for example 6 to 156 weeks for surgery), and the authors note the performance effects in high-grade injuries are less certain.",
  "practicalImplications": "On the sideline, hold the player if any instability is found on examination, and image with weight-bearing radiographs to look for sesamoid migration. Start with rest, ice, compression and elevation for grade I and II injuries, use taping or a stiff-soled shoe on return, and restrict grade III athletes to straight-line running until they can sprint without pain before cutting drills.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: this review supports keeping push-off and cutting strength and range of motion at the centre of the rehabilitation phases, and it notes that higher-grade injuries can reduce performance in as many as 73% of athletes. Use the phased protocols to rebuild toe-off and cutting capacity before full practice.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: the review gives return-to-play criteria by grade, such as minimal pain with full weight-bearing, sprinting and cutting, and a 50 to 60 degree painless first MTP arc. These criteria come from composite sources, so use them as a checklist alongside examination, not as a standard clearance."
 }
}

  "citation": "Gupta A, Singh PK, Xu AL, Bronheim RS, McDaniel CM, Aiyer AA. Turf toe injuries in the athlete: an updated review of treatment options, rehabilitation protocols, and return-to-play outcomes. Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine. 2023. Online publication; volume and pages not printed.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s12178-023-09870-y",
  "abstract": "This review summarises treatment modalities, rehabilitation protocols, return-to-play criteria and performance outcomes after turf toe (first metatarsophalangeal joint sprain) injuries in athletes.",
  "tldr": "Most turf toe injuries are grade I or II and recover without surgery, while grade III injuries may need surgical repair and months of rehabilitation. Use the Anderson grade and the stated phased protocols to plan return, not a single fixed timeline.",
  "methods": "Narrative review of the literature on classification, risk factors, imaging, non-operative and operative management, phased rehabilitation (Tables 4 and 5), return-to-play criteria and performance outcomes. No systematic search is described.",
  "findings": "Under 2% of injuries require surgery, usually grade III injuries with MTP joint damage, bony injury or severe instability. Non-operative rehabilitation has three phases over up to 10 weeks, and operative rehabilitation four phases over up to 20 weeks. Grade I injuries usually return after 3 to 5 days, grade II injuries lose about 2 to 4 weeks, and grade III injuries lose 4 to 6 weeks or more. Median return after non-operative care was 5.85 weeks in one systematic review of 65 patients, against 14.7 weeks after surgery. About 70% of athletes with higher-grade injuries, treated either way, are expected to maintain their level of performance, and one NFL study found power ratings comparable to uninjured controls for low-grade injuries.",
  "limitations": "The review is narrative, so its selection of sources is not reproducible. Many cited return-to-play figures come from small case series, retrospective league data and one systematic review with a wide time range (for example 6 to 156 weeks for surgery), and the authors note the performance effects in high-grade injuries are less certain.",
  "practicalImplications": "On the sideline, hold the player if any instability is found on examination, and image with weight-bearing radiographs to look for sesamoid migration. Start with rest, ice, compression and elevation for grade I and II injuries, use taping or a stiff-soled shoe on return, and restrict grade III athletes to straight-line running until they can sprint without pain before cutting drills.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: this review supports keeping push-off and cutting strength and range of motion at the centre of the rehabilitation phases, and it notes that higher-grade injuries can reduce performance in as many as 73% of athletes. Use the phased protocols to rebuild toe-off and cutting capacity before full practice.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: the review gives return-to-play criteria by grade, such as minimal pain with full weight-bearing, sprinting and cutting, and a 50 to 60 degree painless first MTP arc. These criteria come from composite sources, so use them as a checklist alongside examination, not as a standard clearance."
 }
